It has four courses of double strings, mostly played with a long plectrum, while Cyprus uses a feather. Its role is mainly to accompany Greek traditional music, usually in duet with the Cretan lyra or the Cypriot fiddle.
拉烏託琴見於希臘與賽普勒斯，阿爾巴尼亞稱 llautë、羅馬尼亞稱 lăuta。: The laouto is found in Greece and Cyprus, called llautë in Albania and lăuta in Romania. It belongs to the long-necked fretted lute family and looks like the oud, but steel strings and a long neck mean higher tension and a brighter timbre. Traditionally the strings were gut; today steel or steel-wound nylon is also used. Movable nylon frets and fixed wooden frets serve the modes of Greek traditional music and the makam. The main modern variants are the mainland Greek and the Cretan; the latter has a larger body, a different tuning, and keeps the return tuning. It mainly accompanies Greek traditional music, and in Cyprus it is plucked with a feather and often plays in duet with the fiddle.
